summary: This experimental document defines the Previous-Hop Insertion Block for the DTN Bundle Protocol. A forwarding node inserts an endpoint ID it belongs to, and this is passed to the next node. The receiver can then know where the bundle came from.

eli5.summary: Each stop in a relay writes its own name on the parcel, so the next stop knows who handed it over.

questions: what is phib in bundle protocol
how does a dtn node know the previous hop
subtitle: A one-hop block that tells the next node who just forwarded the bundle.

tldr.problem: In delay-tolerant networks, a receiving node sometimes needs to know which neighbor just forwarded a bundle, especially for flood routing or when the convergence layer cannot provide this information.
tldr.mechanism: The Previous-Hop Insertion Block (PHIB) is inserted by a forwarding node to carry its endpoint identifier (EID), then deleted by the receiver before forwarding onward.
tldr.outcome: Each node can identify its predecessor in the path, enabling intelligent routing decisions like preventing a bundle from bouncing back where it came from.

today: RFC 6259 is an Experimental RFC and part of the DTN standardization effort. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Previous-Hop Insertion Block (PHIB) is an extension block for the DTN Bundle Protocol that lets a forwarding node tell the next node its endpoint identifier (EID). This information is often needed when the receiving node cannot determine where a bundle came from using the convergence layer or other mechanisms.

A typical use case is flood routing: a node floods a bundle to all its neighbors except the one that just sent it (identified via the PHIB). Without this block, a node might accidentally send a bundle back where it came from. The PHIB is also useful when bundles are tunneled across a network, as the tunnel's receiving end cannot determine the tunnel's sending end from the convergence layer alone.

The PHIB can also be used with the DTN Bundle Security Protocol to provide a security-source EID for hop-by-hop authentication.

The lifetime of the PHIB is strictly one hop: it is inserted by the sender, read by the receiver, and then deleted before the bundle is forwarded onward. This ensures each node only knows its immediate predecessor.
sections.eli5: When a relay worker hands off a package, they write their name in a special slot. The next worker reads the name, takes note, and erases it before passing the package along.

sections.title: Previous-Hop Block Structure
sections.content:
The PHIB follows the standard Canonical Bundle Block Format. The block type code for PHIB is 0x05. The block processing control flags MUST have the "Discard block if it can't be processed" flag set, ensuring that nodes that do not support PHIB will not mishandle the bundle.

The EID of the inserting node can be represented in two ways. If the node's EID is already in the dictionary of the bundle's primary block (for example, as the source, current custodian, or report-to endpoint), the PHIB MAY reference it using the optional Block EID-reference field. In this case, the block has no other data.

If the node's EID is not already in the dictionary, the PHIB MUST carry the EID explicitly as block-type-specific data fields: the scheme name (such as "dtn") and the scheme-specific part (such as "node1"), both null-terminated strings. These two approaches are mutually exclusive: the PHIB contains either a reference or explicit data, never both.
sections.eli5: The block is a message saying "I just sent this package." If your name is already listed in the bundle for another reason, the block points to it. Otherwise, the block carries your full name.

sections.title: Insertion, Forwarding, and Removal
sections.content:
When transmitting a bundle, a node MAY include a PHIB based on local policy and the routing protocol in use.

When forwarding a bundle, a node MUST delete any PHIB present from the received bundle (to enforce the one-hop lifetime). The node MAY then insert a new PHIB carrying one of its own EIDs, following these rules: if the node belongs to exactly one endpoint, it MAY insert one PHIB with that endpoint's EID. If the node belongs to multiple endpoints, it MAY insert multiple PHIBs, but each must carry a unique singleton EID of the forwarding node, and each must be expressible in a URI scheme that either the next-hop node supports or that matches the bundle's destination.

When receiving a bundle with a PHIB, the node makes the previous-hop EID available for routing decisions and then deletes the PHIB before forwarding. If the bundle is the final destination, the receiving application may optionally be given the previous-hop EID.
sections.eli5: As a package travels, each worker removes the old name tag and adds their own before passing it along, so each tag only travels one step.

sections.title: Security and Integrity
sections.content:
The PHIB can be protected by the DTN Bundle Security Protocol. When a ciphersuite uses strict canonicalization (such as BAB-HMAC for hop-by-hop authentication), the PHIB is included in the integrity calculation, so it is protected from the forwarding node to the adjacent receiving node.

Ciphersuites using mutable canonicalization deliberately exclude the PHIB from the integrity hash, allowing the block to change at each hop without breaking end-to-end authentication. This is correct behavior, as the PHIB is expected to change at each hop.

If end-to-end confidentiality of the PHIB is needed, an Extension Security Block can encrypt it separately from the payload. Importantly, nodes should be aware that a forwarding node might falsely claim a certain EID in the PHIB, which could be used to subvert routing strategies. The BAB ciphersuite can authenticate the PHIB's origin, but does not prevent deliberate misrepresentation by a compromised node.
sections.eli5: The name tag can be protected with a seal, so nobody can forge it or change it en route. But each hop is allowed to replace the old tag with a new one.

sections.title: Routing Applications
sections.content:
The primary use of PHIB is flood routing. When a node receives a bundle, it floods it to all neighbors except the one identified in the PHIB, preventing loops and wasted forwarding.

A second use case is tunnel support. When DTN bundles are encapsulated and tunneled across a network, the node at the receiving end of the tunnel cannot determine the tunnel sender's EID from convergence-layer information alone. The PHIB allows the tunnel sender to provide its EID explicitly.

PHIB can also carry the security-source EID for Bundle Authentication Block ciphersuites, offering an alternative to EID references or key-information parameters.
sections.eli5: The previous-hop information helps routing make smart decisions, like not sending a package back to where it came from, and helps special delivery modes like tunneling work correctly.

fields.name: Flags (SDNV)
fields.desc: Control flags; must set "Discard if not processed".

fields.name: EID-ref (optional)
fields.desc: Reference to an EID already in the dictionary, if present.

fields.name: Block Data Length (SDNV)
fields.desc: Zero if EID referenced, non-zero if scheme and SSP follow.
